What a downcode costs a practice: the count, the dollars, and the staff time behind them

When a payer pays an office visit one level below the level billed, the practice usually sees an ordinary payment. The 835 remittance file it already receives holds both codes, so plain code can count every downcode, price the gap against the contract, and run a burden clock on the staff work it takes to get the money back. The same counts are what a practice brings to a contract renewal.

Built by Serious AI Partners on three measures: how often payers pay a visit below the level billed, the dollars between the two codes, and the staff time and waiting it takes to recover them. Everything runs on made-up sample data for six practices, and section 2 shows one of them a month at a time.

The finding, on made-up sample data
$38,719 a yearpaid below the level billed at a sample four-physician practice, $9,680 per physician
$31,673 a yearof staff time to appeal each one, for an expected $10,841 back
$6,695 a yearnet after batching each payer's downcodes: $4,146 of staff time for the same $10,841

One claim at a time, a downcode costs less to accept than to fight. Appealing one by one takes staff time worth about three times what it brings back here, and more than it brings back even at a 68.6% win rate ($32,426 of staff time for $26,561) [9]. So practices quietly absorb them, and automatic downcoding pays for the payer even when the practice would win the appeal. Fighting one by one breaks even only when the whole round trip takes under about 29 minutes of staff time per downcode at a 28% win rate, or about 72 minutes at 68.6%. The sample's inputs put it near 85 minutes, and a practice's own timed steps would settle it.

For a practice, the answer is to catch every downcode with code at almost no cost, send each payer one batch a month, and take the payer's pattern to contract renewal in place of fighting line by line.

Our arithmetic on sample data: the practice's August 2026 remits times 12, 28% of appeals paid [1], staff time at $31.43 an hour [10]. Section 2 shows the month, and Scale it applies the sample's pace to a group your size.

Computed in your browser from all 124 sample 835 files: 14,368 service lines from six made-up practices. The switches in section 1 carry through to everything here.

Scale it: the sample's pace at your size

Our arithmetic on made-up sample data, at the six sample practices' 90-day pace: $6,309 per physician per year. It counts only high-level office visits (level 4 and 5) that the sample's payers paid below the level billed, and leaves out other services, denials and underpayments, so a practice's own payers set the real figure. The revenue input defaults to MGMA's 2025 figure for primary care total medical revenue per physician, $760,383 [22]. Change it to your practice's number. The sample practice in section 1 runs higher in its August 2026 remits than over its full 90 days ($29,958 a year at the 90-day pace), because Sample Plan C's review starts August 1.

What the month says, on these inputs

59 of 629 high-level visits on the August 2026 remits came back paid below the level billed, $3,226.59 at contract, or about $38,719 a year ($9,680 per physician), and 21 of the 59 carried no code that says so. Appealing each one, with a model drafting and a coder confirming, takes about 1,008 staff hours a year ($31,673) to bring back an expected $10,841. With a coder writing every appeal by hand it takes 1,893 hours a year ($59,488). That fits what one Illinois clinic reported: the cost of fighting came close to the revenue lost [1].

Sending each payer one batch a month changes the math, to about 132 hours a year ($4,146) for the same expected $10,841, if a batch is paid as often as an appeal (an assumption a pilot tests). Indiana's and Virginia's new laws allow batched appeals [5] [6], and so would the AMA's model state bill [6]. Figures a year are the month's remits times 12, our arithmetic on sample data.

3.Where it stops, and try to break it

What the counts can and can't show, and edits to a remit line that the check does and doesn't survive.

What the counts can and can't show

  • A payer that leaves the billed code off. The remit then carries only the lower code, and the check can't see the change. Matching each remit line to the claim the practice sent (the 837, by account number) closes the gap. Try it on the right.
  • A downcode can be right. The count shows how often a payer paid less than the level billed, and some of those notes support only the lower level. The note reading in section 1 and the appeal outcomes separate the two.
  • The burden column is only as good as its minutes. Until the steps are timed in real practices, it rests on one clinic's two hours [1], CAQH's status-check time [8] and our placeholders (Q1).
  • Rates missing from a fee schedule. The downcode still counts, from the two codes. The dollar column stays blank for that payer until the rate is loaded, so the visible cost runs low.

Nothing goes to a payer until a person signs

The model reads notes and drafts wording. It never decides an appeal, never submits one, never estimates a minute or a dollar, and never changes a record in the practice's systems.

Try to break it

Each edit changes the remit line for the first sample claim (account S102463). The same plain code as section 1 reads it, in your browser.

5.One way to test it, if useful

Small and fast, with numbers before and after, on your own remits.

FirstA short walkthrough with you

You walk this page with us and correct Q1 to Q5, especially the minutes and the payers.

Then90 days of your remits, de-identified

Your billing team exports 90 days of remittance detail with names, member IDs and full dates removed (HIPAA Safe Harbor [15]), plus the fee schedule. The check's export reader refuses any file that still carries an identifier column or a full date. The team also times 20 downcodes through its real steps on a simple log.

ThenOne page for your practice

The three measures by payer and physician, the notes worth pulling, and what batching each payer's downcodes would save. You judge whether it is worth taking to the next contract renewal.

What would prove it wrong

  • Your payers leave the billed code off most changed lines. Then the remit alone undercounts, and the check needs each practice's claim file matched by account.
  • Timed appeals come in well under 30 minutes. Then the hidden-burden column shrinks, and the case rests on frequency and dollars.
  • Downcodes stay under 1% of high-level visits at every payer. Then there is little to report, and the same files point to other leaks.

If your practice engages us for the build, part of our fee rides on these numbers moving. We stake the result.

How we would build it

The technical detail behind the demo: accuracy on the sample, the pipeline end to end, the integration tiers and model cost. Each part opens with a click.

A.Accuracy and calibration on the sampleThe counting is checked against the generator's answer key. The note reading and the minutes need a pilot to calibrate.

The sample generator plants every downcode on purpose and writes an answer key, plus decoys the check has to tell apart: an old rate at one payer, a few short payments, denials and modifier-only changes. Your browser recomputes this from the 835 files on this page.

Sample practiceDowncodes plantedFound by the checkGap at contractFlagged on the remit
The note reading, before it reads anything unasked

The model's reading is scripted on this page, so the sample can't measure it. In a pilot, a certified coder reads a random set of flagged notes without seeing the model's call, and the model must clear this bar before its reading counts (our proposal):

  • Agrees with the coder on supports or does not support in at least 90% of 100 notes.
  • Says supports on a note the coder rejects no more than 2 times in 100, since that error sends a weak appeal.
  • Every quote it gives appears in the note word for word, checked by code (the Plan C claim in section 1 shows a misread time caught this way).
The minutes, before they go on a results page

Every minute on this page is an input, and none comes from a model. In a pilot each billing team logs start and stop times on 20 downcodes, step by step. The median per step replaces the placeholder, and the results page reports the number of timed cases beside each figure.

A step timed on fewer than 10 cases keeps its placeholder label.

B.The pipeline, end to endEleven steps. Code does every count, dollar and minute, a model reads and writes words, and a person signs.
  1. ReceiveCodeThe 835 files from the clearinghouse, or a de-identified export.
  2. ReadCodeEvery service line: payer, physician, codes, adjustments.
  3. CompareCodeCode billed (SVC06) against code paid (SVC01).
  4. PriceCodeContract rate for the code billed, minus the allowed amount.
  5. CountCodeFrequency, gap and flagged share, by payer and physician.
  6. Pull the notePerson or codeFlagged visits only, from the EHR.
  7. Read the noteModelThe decision-making elements and total time, each with a quote.
  8. Verify and apply the ruleCodeEvery quote must appear in the note. Two of three elements, or time, sets the level.
  9. DecidePersonAppeal, write off or escalate, by the billing manager.
  10. DraftModel + codeThe model writes the sentences, code fills every number.
  11. ClockCodeTimed minutes and days for each step, totaled per payer.
Plain code, no model, same answer every timeA model call, structured output with quotesA person

What stays out of the model's hands

  • Every number. The model never counts, prices, totals or times anything.
  • The level. The model reports what the note shows, element by element. Code applies the AMA rule [7], and a coder confirms.
  • Unverified reading. A reading counts only when its quote appears word for word in the note.
  • The decision. A person signs every appeal.

How the data moves

  • A first look runs on a de-identified export (HIPAA Safe Harbor, dates cut to the year), so no protected health information changes hands.
  • Work on a practice's own notes runs under its business associate agreement, and notes reach a model only where that agreement covers the model provider. Otherwise a coder reads every note.
C.Three integration tiers, least to most change for a practiceAnd what each one asks of your team.
Tier 1, no integration

A de-identified export, once a quarter

The billing team exports 90 days of remittance detail with identifiers and full dates removed, plus the fee schedule. We run the check and the clock, and report.

Practice IT gives

Nothing. It is a report the billing team already knows how to run.

Timing

Days.

Tier 2, read-only

The 835 files, weekly

The 835s the clearinghouse already delivers, copied each week to a secure folder the check reads, under a business associate agreement. The billing team gets a weekly alert and pulls notes for flagged visits only.

Practice IT gives
  • A scoped, read-only drop of 835 files.
  • The fee schedule, and the agreement.
Timing

One to two weeks.

Tier 3, in the workflow

Live in the billing workflow

Alerts land where the billing manager works, notes for flagged visits come through read-only EHR access, appeal drafts wait for sign-off, and the clock times each step as it happens.

Practice IT gives
  • Read-only EHR access scoped to flagged visits.
  • A security review and a test environment.
Timing

Weeks, set by the practice's change process more than the build.
